transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, I guess what brings me in is that since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day long, kinda like I still have a crew waiting on me. Which is funny, because my old foreman, Tommy—he actually called me out of the blue on Tuesday. Moved down to Florida, bought himself a boat. A pontoon, I think he said. I don't know why anyone buys a pontoon, honestly. They're basically just floating patios. You can't really fish off 'em right, and the steering is terrible on those things. But anyway, yeah, I was out back yesterday fixing the latch on the shed door because the wind keeps catching it, and my wife comes out and tells me I need to come talk to somebody because I'm driving her crazy pacing around the house.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety when you're not actively doing something?

Oh, yeah, definitely. If I have to just sit there, like... well, like sitting through a quiet meeting or a church talk, I feel like I’ve just got to shift around in the seat. I'll be tapping my foot, or I get this urge to just get up and stretch my legs even when I know I'm supposed to stay put. 

Actually, speaking of church, Pastor Dave has been going on these really long sermons lately. Last Sunday he talked about the new roof fund for a solid twenty minutes. Which, I get it, the roof leaks. It leaked right on Mrs. Gable's hat last month. It was this big pink thing with feathers, kinda looked like a flamingo sitting on her head. My wife elbowed me because I was chuckling, but you can't just wear a flamingo hat and not expect folks to notice, you know? And they want thirty grand for the shingles, which is a total rip-off if you ask me. I told Dave I could get my old crew to do it for half that, but... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, sitting still. Yeah, I just can't do it. My foot just keeps tapping the whole time he's up there talking.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or blurting out answers before they finish speaking?

Yeah, I do that a lot, actually. Like, we have this storytelling group at the community center on Thursdays—well, usually Thursdays, except last week because they had the floors waxed. You wouldn't believe the smell of that wax, it gave half the room a headache. They used this cheap industrial stuff instead of the good polish. I told the guy at the front desk, I said, "You're gonna give the seniors asthma attacks." But anyway, in those storytelling meetings, I'll just jump right in or answer before the person even finishes their story. It just pops out of my mouth. And then I realize I totally cut them off and ruined the punchline, and I feel really bad about it. But by then it's too late, the words are already out there. Kind of like when you spill paint on a carpet, you know? Once it's down, you're just scrubbing at it making it worse.
Do you often find yourself unable to finish the things you start?

Yeah, that happens all the time. Like, my wife will ask me to do a few things around the house—fix the gate, sweep the porch, put the tools away. And I'll go out there and start on the gate. I'll get it maybe halfway done, but then I'll see some weeds over by the steps that need pulling. And you know how weeds are, especially crabgrass. Crabgrass is the worst. Once it gets a hold in your yard, it just spreads like wildfire. My neighbor, Gary, he tried using that spray stuff on his crabgrass, but it just ended up killing his petunias. He was so mad. His wife loves those petunias. They buy flats of them every spring from that nursery down on Route 9. The guy who runs that place, I think his name is Sal, he used to be a mechanic before he bought the nursery. Always has grease under his fingernails, even when he's handling flowers. It's the funniest thing. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll go to pull the weeds, and the gate is just sitting there half-fixed, the porch isn't swept, and the tools are just left out in the yard. My wife gets so frustrated with me about it.
Do you often act on impulse in social situations, like suddenly deciding to do something without thinking it through?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm not really one to just jump up and do something crazy at a party or anything. I'm usually pretty content just hanging back. Like at the retirement party they threw for me a few years back. It was down at the VFW hall. They had this big sheet cake, half chocolate, half vanilla. The icing was that really stiff, sugary kind that kind of crunches when you bite into it. I'm not a big fan of that icing. I prefer a buttercream, you know? My sister-in-law makes a great buttercream. She puts a little bit of almond extract in it, which sounds weird, but it really gives it a nice flavor. She made my nephew's wedding cake with it. He got married out in Colorado, up in the mountains. Beautiful scenery, but the altitude really got to me. I was huffing and puffing just walking from the car to the ceremony. 

But anyway, no, I don't really do things without thinking about them first when I'm around other people. I'm pretty steady that way.
Have you noticed that your behavior or inability to focus has caused problems for you at home, with friends, or in other areas of your life?

Yeah, I guess it has caused some friction. My wife actually had to take over keeping the calendar for us. She checks behind me on pretty much everything now, paying bills, making sure I locked the back door... which reminds me, we had to get a new lock for that door last month. The old one just froze up completely. I tried spraying WD-40 in it, but it didn't do a lick of good. You know, they say WD-40 is a lubricant, but it's really a water displacer. That's what the 'WD' stands for—Water Displacement, 40th formula. A guy at the hardware store told me that once. He said people use it on everything, but it actually attracts dust if you use it on door hinges. You're supposed to use silicone spray or graphite powder. I bought a little tube of graphite powder, the kind you squeeze, and it got everywhere. My hands were silver for two days. I looked like the Tin Man from The Wizard of Oz. My grandkids thought it was hilarious. They love that movie, though I always thought the flying monkeys were a little too scary for kids. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, problems. Yeah, my wife checks up on me. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and my garden group more than once for letting people down. I'll forget I promised to bring the folding chairs, or I'll show up on the wrong day. It's embarrassing, really.
Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're not able to keep busy or complete tasks?

I don't really know about anxious. I mean, I guess I don't feel overwhelmed if I'm not doing something. I actually like sitting down in my recliner with a cup of coffee. It's one of those big recliners, you know, the kind with the lever on the side. My son got it for me for Father's Day a couple of years ago. He bought it from that furniture place out by the highway, the one with the giant inflatable gorilla on the roof. I don't know why they use a gorilla. Maybe because their prices are bananas? I asked the salesman that once, and he just looked at me like I had two heads. Anyway, the chair is great. It's microfiber, so it's really easy to clean if you spill something. Which is good, because I spilled a whole mug of tomato soup on it last winter. Campbell's, the kind you mix with milk, not water. It's so much creamier that way. 

But yeah, I don't really get stressed out if I'm just sitting still and not getting things done. I don't mind taking a break.
Do you think your inability to slow down and complete tasks is affecting your relationships with family and friends?

Well, yeah, it definitely gets on my wife's nerves. Like, she'll ask me to do a few things around the house—fix the latch on the side gate, sweep off the back porch, put my tools back in the shed. And I have every intention of doing it all. But I'll get out there, get the gate maybe halfway fixed, and then I'll notice the weeds growing up around the azalea bushes. We planted those azaleas when we first moved in, oh, thirty-some years ago now. The soil here is pretty acidic, which they love. You have to be careful with azaleas, though, because if they get too much direct afternoon sun, the leaves will scorch. My neighbor, Frank, he planted his right out in the middle of the yard, full sun, and they just shriveled up. I told him he needed to put them under the oak tree, but Frank's stubborn. He used to work down at the auto plant before it closed. He's got this old Chevy Nova he's been restoring for a decade. Beautiful car, cherry red. He let me ride in it once, but the suspension is so stiff you feel every single pebble on the road. My back was killing me for a week after that. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the chores. So I'll wander off to pull the weeds by the bushes, and before I know it, the afternoon's gone. The gate's only half done, the porch isn't swept, and my tools are just sitting out in the yard. And she gets pretty frustrated with me over it, which I understand. It's just hard to stick with the one thing she asked me to do until it's finished.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

Oh, all the time. It doesn't take much to pull me away. Like, if I'm sitting down trying to paint—I do a little watercolor, mostly landscapes—or if I'm trying to plan out one of those little short stories I like to write, the slightest thing will just derail me. I'll hear a delivery truck rumble past outside, or I'll suddenly remember I need to prune the hydrangeas in the garden, and boom, my mind jumps right over there. 

Speaking of trucks, the mail carrier we have now drives one of those new electric vans. It's so quiet, you don't even know he's coming until he's right at the mailbox. The old one used to rattle and clank so much you could hear it three streets over. Our carrier's name is Dave. Nice guy, always wears shorts even when it's freezing out. I asked him about it once, and he said his legs don't get cold, just his hands. He wears these fingerless gloves, the kind with the little mitten flap you can pull over. My grandmother used to knit those for us when we were kids. We called them glittens. She'd use this really itchy wool, though, so we hated wearing them. 

But yeah, what was the question? Oh, distractions. Yeah, if I hear that truck or think about the garden, I completely lose where I was with my painting or my story. I'll look back at the paper and have no idea what I was trying to do.
Do you find it difficult to focus or sit still in all situations, or are there certain places or activities where you can concentrate without much trouble?

Well, I'd say it depends. If I'm out in the garden or tinkering with something, I'm okay. But if I have to sit through something quiet, like a long meeting or a church talk... oh boy. I just feel like I've got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch, even when I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen. 

We go to the First Presbyterian over on Elm Street. Beautiful old building, stained glass windows and everything. They replaced the pews a few years ago, though, and I swear they put in the hardest wood they could find. The old ones had these red velvet cushions that were starting to wear out—you could see the foam poking through on the end where Mrs. Higgins always sat. She's been going there since the fifties, I think. Always wears a hat. You don't see ladies wearing hats to church much anymore, do you? Just her. She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. 

But anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.
Have you always been this way, or did you notice these difficulties with focusing and sitting still developing at some point in your life?

Well, yeah, it's pretty much been this way my whole life, near as I can tell. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my parents I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before they even called on me, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I ran out for recess. 

Recess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big asphalt lot behind the school. You had to be careful, though, because if you tripped on that asphalt, it would tear your knees right up. I remember Jimmy Peterson took a bad spill once, scraped himself up so bad his mom had to come get him. Jimmy’s mom drove this huge station wagon with the wood paneling on the side. You don't see cars like that anymore. Now everybody drives those little crossover SUVs that all look exactly the same. You walk out of the grocery store and you can't even tell which one is yours. My wife put a bright yellow antenna topper on ours—a little smiley face—just so we could find it in the lot at the Piggly Wiggly. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, it's always been there. Ever since I was a little kid, just losing things and having a hard time staying on track.
Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and sitting still are affecting your overall well-being or daily life in a major way?

Well, it's definitely a hassle, I guess you could say. It's gotten to the point where my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me for just about everything. Which is a shame, because I used to try to keep my own pocket planner. I had this really nice leather one, dark brown, with my initials stamped in gold on the front. My daughter bought it for me for Father's Day a few years back. She got it at one of those little boutique shops downtown, the ones that sell artisanal soaps and candles that smell like pine needles and campfire smoke. I love that smell. Reminds me of when we used to take the kids camping up near the lake. We had this old canvas tent that weighed an absolute ton, and if it rained, you had to make sure you didn't touch the sides or the water would seep right through. 

We used to cook hotdogs on sticks we found in the woods. You had to find the perfect stick, you know? Not too dry or it would catch fire, and it had to have a nice little fork at the end to hold the hotdog. Kids today, they have those metal extendable roasting forks you buy at the sporting goods store. Takes all the fun out of it, if you ask me. 

But anyway, yeah, the calendar. I'd write things in that planner and then just forget to look at it, or I'd leave it on the workbench and lose it under a pile of sandpaper. So now she handles all that. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down—forgetting I was supposed to bring the mulch, or showing up on the wrong Tuesday for the planning committee. So, yeah, it definitely gets in the way of things.
Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble paying attention or that you act on impulse without thinking?

Well, I don't really know if I could pick just one. I mean, they both seem to happen, don't they? Like, I'll be trying to pay attention to something, and then before I know it, I'm doing something else entirely without even thinking about it. Like last week, I was supposed to be fixing the hinge on the back gate. The screws had gotten all rusted out from all that rain we had in April. 

April was just awful this year, wasn't it? Seemed like it rained every single day. My tomatoes didn't know what to do with themselves. They got that blossom end rot because the soil was just too damp for too long. You have to be careful with tomatoes, they like water but they don't like wet feet, as my grandfather used to say. He had this massive garden out behind his house. Grew everything. Corn, beans, squash. He used to make these little scarecrows out of old flannel shirts and pie tins to keep the crows away. The pie tins would clank together in the wind. It was a nice sound, actually. Very peaceful. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the gate. Yeah, I went out to fix the gate, and I saw a weed in the flowerbed, so I pulled it. And then I saw another one, and the next thing I know, I've spent two hours pulling weeds and the gate is still broken. So I don't know if that's me not paying attention to the gate, or just impulsively pulling weeds. It all just sort of blends together for me.
Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble sitting still and being patient, or that you have trouble paying attention to details and following through on instructions?

Well, it's funny you ask it that way, because I think it's a little bit of both, honestly, but maybe more the details part. Like, when I'm helping out with the volunteer storytelling flyers over at the community center, or even just jotting down my garden notes, I'm always messing something up. I'll miss putting the date on the flyer, or I'll leave out somebody's name entirely. Or out in the garden, I'll measure the fertilizer wrong, even though I swear I just looked right at the instructions. 

I used to use this liquid fertilizer that came in a bright green bottle. It smelled awful, like fish, but boy, did it make the hydrangeas bloom. My grandmother had hydrangeas all along the front of her porch. Huge blue ones. She said the trick was putting rusty nails in the soil to change the color. I don't know if that actually works or if it's just an old wives' tale, but she swore by it. She kept all her rusty nails in this old Folgers coffee can in the shed. You know the ones, the metal cans with the plastic lids? People used to keep everything in those. Screws, buttons, bacon grease... you name it. Now coffee comes in those bags that never seal right once you open them. I end up spilling coffee grounds all over the counter every single morning. My wife just sighs and hands me the sponge. She's a saint, really. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, following through and details. Yeah, I'll think I looked a flyer over perfectly, or read the garden notes right, and then someone points out I completely missed a whole section. So I guess the attention to detail is definitely a big part of it.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to focus or sit still over the years, or has it remained relatively consistent?

Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. 

Speaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. 

But anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. 

Recess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. 

So, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD, or do you have any family members with the condition?

Well, no, I've never been diagnosed with it or anything like that. Neither has anyone in my family, as far as I know. My brother, though, he was always bouncing off the walls, but back then they just called it having too much energy. He played football in high school. Linebacker. He was tough as nails, my brother. Broke his collarbone twice and just kept on playing. 

Football was different back then, you know? The helmets didn't have all that padding they do now. They were practically just plastic shells with a little bit of foam inside. And the coaches, they wouldn't let you drink water during practice. Said it made you soft. Can you imagine that today? With all the heatstroke and everything, they'd be sued in a heartbeat. We used to sneak over to the hose behind the fieldhouse when the coach wasn't looking. That water tasted like rubber and rust, but it was the best thing I ever drank. 

My brother actually got a scholarship to play at a small college up state, but he ended up blowing out his knee his freshman year. It was a shame, really. He loved the game. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. Sells everything from two-by-fours to those little tiny screws you need for eyeglasses. I was just in there last week looking for a specific kind of washer for the lawnmower. 

Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, diagnoses and family. No, no one's ever been officially diagnosed or treated for anything like that. Just the way we've always been, I guess.
Are there any activities that you find so engaging or enjoyable that you can focus on them for long periods of time without getting distracted or feeling restless?

Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. I'll start humming to myself, or talking out loud, or I'll just have to get up and mess with something in the room. 

I used to sketch a lot more when I was younger. Mostly birds. We had this big oak tree in the backyard, and the blue jays would just swarm the feeder. Blue jays are mean birds, though. They'll chase off all the cardinals and the finches just to get to the sunflower seeds. We used to buy the black oil sunflower seeds in these massive fifty-pound bags from the feed store down on Route 9. 

That feed store is gone now, though. They tore it down to build one of those giant chain pharmacies. You know the ones, where they sell everything from milk to lawn chairs, but there's only ever one person working the register? The lines are always terrible. And the fluorescent lights in there give me a headache. I miss the old feed store. It smelled like molasses and dust, and the guy who ran it, old Mr. Henderson, he had this three-legged dog that would just sleep on the porch all day. 

I think the dog's name was Buster. Or maybe Barnaby? Something with a B. He lost the leg getting hit by a tractor, they said. But he got around just fine. Dogs are resilient like that. They don't sit around feeling sorry for themselves, they just figure out how to walk on three legs and get on with it. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the quiet hobbies. Yeah, reading or sketching, I just end up fidgeting or getting up to fiddle with the blinds or something. I just can't stay settled with it.
Do you think your difficulties are more related to not being able to pay attention to details or to being overly active and restless?

Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but the details really do trip me up quite a bit. Like, when I help out with the volunteer storytelling flyers down at the center, or when I'm writing down my garden notes, I’ll just completely miss a date, or I'll leave out somebody's name. Or I'll measure something wrong out in the yard, even though I could have sworn I looked it over real careful. 

Speaking of the yard, I was measuring for some new tomato stakes recently. I grow those big heirloom tomatoes, the Brandywines. They get so heavy you have to tie them up to the stakes with strips of old pantyhose so the stems don't snap. My grandmother taught me that trick. She had a garden the size of a baseball diamond out behind her place. Grew absolutely everything under the sun. Corn, squash, pole beans. She used to can her own green beans in those heavy glass mason jars. You'd sit in the kitchen and just wait to hear that sharp little "pop" sound when the lids sealed as they cooled down on the counter. 

We kept all those jars down in the root cellar. That cellar always smelled like damp earth and old potatoes. There was an old iron coal chute down there, too, from back before they put the oil furnace in. The coal truck would pull right up to the side of the house and just rattle all that coal right down the chute. It made a terrible racket, and the coal dust would get on absolutely everything. You'd be wiping black soot off the windowsills for a week after a delivery. 

Wait, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Losing the track. What was it you were asking me about? Oh, right, the details or being restless. Yeah, it's the details that get me. Just missing dates on those flyers and messing up my garden measurements, mostly, no matter how hard I try to double-check things.
Do you think your difficulties with focusing and sitting still might be related to ADHD?

Well, I don't really know. I mean, I've heard the term before, mostly on the television or when people talk about kids in school. But for me? I'm not sure. It's just... the way I am, I guess. 

Speaking of television, they just don't make shows like they used to, do they? Everything now is all these reality programs with people yelling at each other on islands or in big houses. Or it's those crime shows where they solve a murder in forty-five minutes using some fancy computer that can zoom in on a reflection in a puddle from a satellite. Back in the day, you had proper stories. Like *Gunsmoke* or *The Andy Griffith Show*. 

Andy Griffith, now there was a show. Just a sheriff and his boy, and Barney Fife causing all sorts of trouble. Don Knotts was a genius, absolute genius. The way he could just shake and look nervous, it was pure comedy. My dad used to laugh so hard at Barney Fife that he'd start coughing and have to go get a glass of water. 

My dad drank a lot of water. Always had a big glass jar of it in the fridge with a slice of lemon in it. He said the lemon cut the dust from the factory. He worked at the old textile mill over in the next county. Spun cotton mostly, I think. The noise in that place was deafening. He had to wear these big heavy earmuffs all day, but he still lost most of his hearing by the time he was fifty. He used to say he didn't mind, though, because it meant he didn't have to listen to my mother's soap operas. 

She loved her stories, my mother. *Days of Our Lives*, *General Hospital*. She'd iron clothes in the living room just so she wouldn't miss a minute of it. The smell of hot iron on damp cotton... that always takes me right back to being a kid. 

But, uh... I lost the thread again, didn't I? You were asking about that ADHD thing. Yeah, I really don't know if that's what it is. I haven't really thought about it having a name like that.
Do you think your main difficulty is with staying focused on tasks or with feeling restless and fidgety?

Well, I'd say the restlessness is a pretty big one for me. Like, if I'm sitting through a quiet meeting or a church talk, I just feel like I’ve got to shift around in my seat, or I'll start tapping my foot. I just get this overwhelming urge to get up and stretch, even when I know I really should just stay put and be polite. 

Speaking of church, our pastor, Reverend Davis, he can really stretch a sermon out. Nice man, though. His wife plays the organ. It's one of those beautiful old pipe organs, you know the kind? With all the wooden pedals and the big brass pipes up on the wall. They had to get a specialist all the way from Chicago just to come tune the thing last spring. Cost the congregation a small fortune. We had to do a whole month of bake sales just to cover the travel expenses for the tuning fella. 

I made three cherry pies for that sale. Used my mother's old recipe. The secret is a little bit of almond extract in the filling, it really makes the cherries pop. And you have to use real lard in the crust. People are so scared of lard these days, but it's what makes the pastry actually flake. You cut it in ice-cold with a pastry blender, and you have to use ice water, too, or the fat melts before it even hits the oven... 

Wait, goodness, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry, I get to talking about baking and I just lose the whole point of the conversation. You were asking about the fidgeting. But yes, it's definitely the restlessness. Sitting in those pews or anywhere quiet, I just can't keep my feet still to save my life.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety when you're not actively doing something?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: Sitting through a quiet meeting or church talk, I feel like I’ve got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch even when I know I should stay put.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel restless or fidgety when not actively doing something. This maps perfectly to the symptom 'Feeling_Restless' (S012).

patient.answer:
Oh, yeah, definitely. If I have to just sit there, like... well, like sitting through a quiet meeting or a church talk, I feel like I’ve just got to shift around in the seat. I'll be tapping my foot, or I get this urge to just get up and stretch my legs even when I know I'm supposed to stay put. 

Actually, speaking of church, Pastor Dave has been going on these really long sermons lately. Last Sunday he talked about the new roof fund for a solid twenty minutes. Which, I get it, the roof leaks. It leaked right on Mrs. Gable's hat last month. It was this big pink thing with feathers, kinda looked like a flamingo sitting on her head. My wife elbowed me because I was chuckling, but you can't just wear a flamingo hat and not expect folks to notice, you know? And they want thirty grand for the shingles, which is a total rip-off if you ask me. I told Dave I could get my old crew to do it for half that, but... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, sitting still. Yeah, I just can't do it. My foot just keeps tapping the whole time he's up there talking.

doctor.intent: determine presence of impulsivity

patient.answer: Yeah, I do that a lot, actually. Like, we have this storytelling group at the community center on Thursdays—well, usually Thursdays, except last week because they had the floors waxed. You wouldn't believe the smell of that wax, it gave half the room a headache. They used this cheap industrial stuff instead of the good polish. I told the guy at the front desk, I said, "You're gonna give the seniors asthma attacks." But anyway, in those storytelling meetings, I'll just jump right in or answer before the person even finishes their story. It just pops out of my mouth. And then I realize I totally cut them off and ruined the punchline, and I feel really bad about it. But by then it's too late, the words are already out there. Kind of like when you spill paint on a carpet, you know? Once it's down, you're just scrubbing at it making it worse.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has difficulty with task completion

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have trouble finishing things I start, which directly maps to the symptom of failing to follow through on instructions or finish chores/duties.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that happens all the time. Like, my wife will ask me to do a few things around the house—fix the gate, sweep the porch, put the tools away. And I'll go out there and start on the gate. I'll get it maybe halfway done, but then I'll see some weeds over by the steps that need pulling. And you know how weeds are, especially crabgrass. Crabgrass is the worst. Once it gets a hold in your yard, it just spreads like wildfire. My neighbor, Gary, he tried using that spray stuff on his crabgrass, but it just ended up killing his petunias. He was so mad. His wife loves those petunias. They buy flats of them every spring from that nursery down on Route 9. The guy who runs that place, I think his name is Sal, he used to be a mechanic before he bought the nursery. Always has grease under his fingernails, even when he's handling flowers. It's the funniest thing. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll go to pull the weeds, and the gate is just sitting there half-fixed, the porch isn't swept, and the tools are just left out in the yard. My wife gets so frustrated with me about it.

doctor.intent: determine presence of impulsivity in social interactions beyond interrupting or blurting out
doctor.question: Do you often act on impulse in social situations, like suddenly deciding to do something without thinking it through?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about general impulsivity in social situations, which is not specifically covered by any of the items in my symptom profile (my profile includes blurting answers and difficulty waiting turn, but not general impulsive actions).

patient.answer:
No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm not really one to just jump up and do something crazy at a party or anything. I'm usually pretty content just hanging back. Like at the retirement party they threw for me a few years back. It was down at the VFW hall. They had this big sheet cake, half chocolate, half vanilla. The icing was that really stiff, sugary kind that kind of crunches when you bite into it. I'm not a big fan of that icing. I prefer a buttercream, you know? My sister-in-law makes a great buttercream. She puts a little bit of almond extract in it, which sounds weird, but it really gives it a nice flavor. She made my nephew's wedding cake with it. He got married out in Colorado, up in the mountains. Beautiful scenery, but the altitude really got to me. I was huffing and puffing just walking from the car to the ceremony. 

But anyway, no, I don't really do things without thinking about them first when I'm around other people. I'm pretty steady that way.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me, and I’ve had to apologize to the community center and garden group more than once for letting people down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the symptoms on my daily life, home, and social activities, which corresponds directly to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess it has caused some friction. My wife actually had to take over keeping the calendar for us. She checks behind me on pretty much everything now, paying bills, making sure I locked the back door... which reminds me, we had to get a new lock for that door last month. The old one just froze up completely. I tried spraying WD-40 in it, but it didn't do a lick of good. You know, they say WD-40 is a lubricant, but it's really a water displacer. That's what the 'WD' stands for—Water Displacement, 40th formula. A guy at the hardware store told me that once. He said people use it on everything, but it actually attracts dust if you use it on door hinges. You're supposed to use silicone spray or graphite powder. I bought a little tube of graphite powder, the kind you squeeze, and it got everywhere. My hands were silver for two days. I looked like the Tin Man from The Wizard of Oz. My grandkids thought it was hilarious. They love that movie, though I always thought the flying monkeys were a little too scary for kids. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, problems. Yeah, my wife checks up on me. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and my garden group more than once for letting people down. I'll forget I promised to bring the folding chairs, or I'll show up on the wrong day. It's embarrassing, really.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are associated with emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're not able to keep busy or complete tasks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of anxiety or being overwhelmed when unable to keep busy, which assesses for symptoms of anxiety or emotional dysregulation rather than the specific ADHD symptoms in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
I don't really know about anxious. I mean, I guess I don't feel overwhelmed if I'm not doing something. I actually like sitting down in my recliner with a cup of coffee. It's one of those big recliners, you know, the kind with the lever on the side. My son got it for me for Father's Day a couple of years ago. He bought it from that furniture place out by the highway, the one with the giant inflatable gorilla on the roof. I don't know why they use a gorilla. Maybe because their prices are bananas? I asked the salesman that once, and he just looked at me like I had two heads. Anyway, the chair is great. It's microfiber, so it's really easy to clean if you spill something. Which is good, because I spilled a whole mug of tomato soup on it last winter. Campbell's, the kind you mix with milk, not water. It's so much creamier that way. 

But yeah, I don't really get stressed out if I'm just sitting still and not getting things done. I don't mind taking a break.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
doctor.question: Do you think your inability to slow down and complete tasks is affecting your relationships with family and friends?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: My wife can ask me to fix the gate, sweep the porch, and put the tools away, and I’ll get the gate half done, wander off to pull weeds, and leave the rest sitting there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's inability to complete tasks and how it affects family relationships, which aligns with his difficulty finishing chores requested by his wife.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it definitely gets on my wife's nerves. Like, she'll ask me to do a few things around the house—fix the latch on the side gate, sweep off the back porch, put my tools back in the shed. And I have every intention of doing it all. But I'll get out there, get the gate maybe halfway fixed, and then I'll notice the weeds growing up around the azalea bushes. We planted those azaleas when we first moved in, oh, thirty-some years ago now. The soil here is pretty acidic, which they love. You have to be careful with azaleas, though, because if they get too much direct afternoon sun, the leaves will scorch. My neighbor, Frank, he planted his right out in the middle of the yard, full sun, and they just shriveled up. I told him he needed to put them under the oak tree, but Frank's stubborn. He used to work down at the auto plant before it closed. He's got this old Chevy Nova he's been restoring for a decade. Beautiful car, cherry red. He let me ride in it once, but the suspension is so stiff you feel every single pebble on the road. My back was killing me for a week after that. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the chores. So I'll wander off to pull the weeds by the bushes, and before I know it, the afternoon's gone. The gate's only half done, the porch isn't swept, and my tools are just sitting out in the yard. And she gets pretty frustrated with me over it, which I understand. It's just hard to stick with the one thing she asked me to do until it's finished.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of inattention
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: If I’m trying to paint or plan a story and I hear a truck outside or think of something in the garden, my mind jumps right over there and I lose where I was.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I am easily distracted by things around me, which maps to the Distractibility symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, all the time. It doesn't take much to pull me away. Like, if I'm sitting down trying to paint—I do a little watercolor, mostly landscapes—or if I'm trying to plan out one of those little short stories I like to write, the slightest thing will just derail me. I'll hear a delivery truck rumble past outside, or I'll suddenly remember I need to prune the hydrangeas in the garden, and boom, my mind jumps right over there. 

Speaking of trucks, the mail carrier we have now drives one of those new electric vans. It's so quiet, you don't even know he's coming until he's right at the mailbox. The old one used to rattle and clank so much you could hear it three streets over. Our carrier's name is Dave. Nice guy, always wears shorts even when it's freezing out. I asked him about it once, and he said his legs don't get cold, just his hands. He wears these fingerless gloves, the kind with the little mitten flap you can pull over. My grandmother used to knit those for us when we were kids. We called them glittens. She'd use this really itchy wool, though, so we hated wearing them. 

But yeah, what was the question? Oh, distractions. Yeah, if I hear that truck or think about the garden, I completely lose where I was with my painting or my story. I'll look back at the paper and have no idea what I was trying to do.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent across different settings
doctor.question: Do you find it difficult to focus or sit still in all situations, or are there certain places or activities where you can concentrate without much trouble?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: Sitting through a quiet meeting or church talk, I feel like I’ve got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch even when I know I should stay put.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to sit still or if I find it difficult in certain situations, which aligns with the feeling restless symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I'd say it depends. If I'm out in the garden or tinkering with something, I'm okay. But if I have to sit through something quiet, like a long meeting or a church talk... oh boy. I just feel like I've got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch, even when I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen. 

We go to the First Presbyterian over on Elm Street. Beautiful old building, stained glass windows and everything. They replaced the pews a few years ago, though, and I swear they put in the hardest wood they could find. The old ones had these red velvet cushions that were starting to wear out—you could see the foam poking through on the end where Mrs. Higgins always sat. She's been going there since the fifties, I think. Always wears a hat. You don't see ladies wearing hats to church much anymore, do you? Just her. She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. 

But anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent across their lifetime or have developed more recently
doctor.question: Have you always been this way, or did you notice these difficulties with focusing and sitting still developing at some point in your life?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, my teachers said I was bright but scattered, always losing pencils, calling out answers, and needing reminders to finish my work before recess.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of my symptoms and whether I have always been this way, which corresponds to the childhood onset requirement.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it's pretty much been this way my whole life, near as I can tell. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my parents I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before they even called on me, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I ran out for recess. 

Recess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big asphalt lot behind the school. You had to be careful, though, because if you tripped on that asphalt, it would tear your knees right up. I remember Jimmy Peterson took a bad spill once, scraped himself up so bad his mom had to come get him. Jimmy’s mom drove this huge station wagon with the wood paneling on the side. You don't see cars like that anymore. Now everybody drives those little crossover SUVs that all look exactly the same. You walk out of the grocery store and you can't even tell which one is yours. My wife put a bright yellow antenna topper on ours—a little smiley face—just so we could find it in the lot at the Piggly Wiggly. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, it's always been there. Ever since I was a little kid, just losing things and having a hard time staying on track.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and sitting still are affecting your overall well-being or daily life in a major way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me, and I’ve had to apologize to the community center and garden group more than once for letting people down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how my symptoms are affecting my daily life and overall well-being, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, it's definitely a hassle, I guess you could say. It's gotten to the point where my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me for just about everything. Which is a shame, because I used to try to keep my own pocket planner. I had this really nice leather one, dark brown, with my initials stamped in gold on the front. My daughter bought it for me for Father's Day a few years back. She got it at one of those little boutique shops downtown, the ones that sell artisanal soaps and candles that smell like pine needles and campfire smoke. I love that smell. Reminds me of when we used to take the kids camping up near the lake. We had this old canvas tent that weighed an absolute ton, and if it rained, you had to make sure you didn't touch the sides or the water would seep right through. 

We used to cook hotdogs on sticks we found in the woods. You had to find the perfect stick, you know? Not too dry or it would catch fire, and it had to have a nice little fork at the end to hold the hotdog. Kids today, they have those metal extendable roasting forks you buy at the sporting goods store. Takes all the fun out of it, if you ask me. 

But anyway, yeah, the calendar. I'd write things in that planner and then just forget to look at it, or I'd leave it on the workbench and lose it under a pile of sandpaper. So now she handles all that. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down—forgetting I was supposed to bring the mulch, or showing up on the wrong Tuesday for the planning committee. So, yeah, it definitely gets in the way of things.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to attention or impulsivity
doctor.question: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble paying attention or that you act on impulse without thinking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a general question about whether the patient's primary issue is inattention or impulsivity, which does not map to one specific symptom criterion in the profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't really know if I could pick just one. I mean, they both seem to happen, don't they? Like, I'll be trying to pay attention to something, and then before I know it, I'm doing something else entirely without even thinking about it. Like last week, I was supposed to be fixing the hinge on the back gate. The screws had gotten all rusted out from all that rain we had in April. 

April was just awful this year, wasn't it? Seemed like it rained every single day. My tomatoes didn't know what to do with themselves. They got that blossom end rot because the soil was just too damp for too long. You have to be careful with tomatoes, they like water but they don't like wet feet, as my grandfather used to say. He had this massive garden out behind his house. Grew everything. Corn, beans, squash. He used to make these little scarecrows out of old flannel shirts and pie tins to keep the crows away. The pie tins would clank together in the wind. It was a nice sound, actually. Very peaceful. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the gate. Yeah, I went out to fix the gate, and I saw a weed in the flowerbed, so I pulled it. And then I saw another one, and the next thing I know, I've spent two hours pulling weeds and the gate is still broken. So I don't know if that's me not paying attention to the gate, or just impulsively pulling weeds. It all just sort of blends together for me.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity
doctor.question: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble sitting still and being patient, or that you have trouble paying attention to details and following through on instructions?

target_item.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
target_item.manifestation: When I help with the volunteer storytelling flyers or write down garden notes, I’ll miss a date, leave out a name, or measure something wrong even though I thought I looked it over.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about having trouble paying attention to details, which directly corresponds to this symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you ask it that way, because I think it's a little bit of both, honestly, but maybe more the details part. Like, when I'm helping out with the volunteer storytelling flyers over at the community center, or even just jotting down my garden notes, I'm always messing something up. I'll miss putting the date on the flyer, or I'll leave out somebody's name entirely. Or out in the garden, I'll measure the fertilizer wrong, even though I swear I just looked right at the instructions. 

I used to use this liquid fertilizer that came in a bright green bottle. It smelled awful, like fish, but boy, did it make the hydrangeas bloom. My grandmother had hydrangeas all along the front of her porch. Huge blue ones. She said the trick was putting rusty nails in the soil to change the color. I don't know if that actually works or if it's just an old wives' tale, but she swore by it. She kept all her rusty nails in this old Folgers coffee can in the shed. You know the ones, the metal cans with the plastic lids? People used to keep everything in those. Screws, buttons, bacon grease... you name it. Now coffee comes in those bags that never seal right once you open them. I end up spilling coffee grounds all over the counter every single morning. My wife just sighs and hands me the sponge. She's a saint, really. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, following through and details. Yeah, I'll think I looked a flyer over perfectly, or read the garden notes right, and then someone points out I completely missed a whole section. So I guess the attention to detail is definitely a big part of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent across their lifetime or have changed over time
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to focus or sit still over the years, or has it remained relatively consistent?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, my teachers said I was bright but scattered, always losing pencils, calling out answers, and needing reminders to finish my work before recess.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history and consistency of symptoms over the years, which relates to the childhood onset of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. 

Speaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. 

But anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. 

Recess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. 

So, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are more consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) or another condition
doctor.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD, or do you have any family members with the condition?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past diagnosis, treatment history, and family history of ADHD, which are not covered by any of the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I've never been diagnosed with it or anything like that. Neither has anyone in my family, as far as I know. My brother, though, he was always bouncing off the walls, but back then they just called it having too much energy. He played football in high school. Linebacker. He was tough as nails, my brother. Broke his collarbone twice and just kept on playing. 

Football was different back then, you know? The helmets didn't have all that padding they do now. They were practically just plastic shells with a little bit of foam inside. And the coaches, they wouldn't let you drink water during practice. Said it made you soft. Can you imagine that today? With all the heatstroke and everything, they'd be sued in a heartbeat. We used to sneak over to the hose behind the fieldhouse when the coach wasn't looking. That water tasted like rubber and rust, but it was the best thing I ever drank. 

My brother actually got a scholarship to play at a small college up state, but he ended up blowing out his knee his freshman year. It was a shame, really. He loved the game. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. Sells everything from two-by-fours to those little tiny screws you need for eyeglasses. I was just in there last week looking for a specific kind of washer for the lawnmower. 

Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, diagnoses and family. No, no one's ever been officially diagnosed or treated for anything like that. Just the way we've always been, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperfocus in activities the patient enjoys
doctor.question: Are there any activities that you find so engaging or enjoyable that you can focus on them for long periods of time without getting distracted or feeling restless?

target_item.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I don’t do well with quiet hobbies for long anymore, because even when I’m reading or sketching I start humming, talking to myself, or getting up to mess with something.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's ability to focus on engaging or enjoyable (leisure) activities for long periods without restlessness or distraction, which directly relates to the patient's difficulty engaging in quiet hobbies for long.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. I'll start humming to myself, or talking out loud, or I'll just have to get up and mess with something in the room. 

I used to sketch a lot more when I was younger. Mostly birds. We had this big oak tree in the backyard, and the blue jays would just swarm the feeder. Blue jays are mean birds, though. They'll chase off all the cardinals and the finches just to get to the sunflower seeds. We used to buy the black oil sunflower seeds in these massive fifty-pound bags from the feed store down on Route 9. 

That feed store is gone now, though. They tore it down to build one of those giant chain pharmacies. You know the ones, where they sell everything from milk to lawn chairs, but there's only ever one person working the register? The lines are always terrible. And the fluorescent lights in there give me a headache. I miss the old feed store. It smelled like molasses and dust, and the guy who ran it, old Mr. Henderson, he had this three-legged dog that would just sleep on the porch all day. 

I think the dog's name was Buster. Or maybe Barnaby? Something with a B. He lost the leg getting hit by a tractor, they said. But he got around just fine. Dogs are resilient like that. They don't sit around feeling sorry for themselves, they just figure out how to walk on three legs and get on with it. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the quiet hobbies. Yeah, reading or sketching, I just end up fidgeting or getting up to fiddle with the blinds or something. I just can't stay settled with it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to inattention or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties are more related to not being able to pay attention to details or to being overly active and restless?

target_item.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
target_item.manifestation: When I help with the volunteer storytelling flyers or write down garden notes, I’ll miss a date, leave out a name, or measure something wrong even though I thought I looked it over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the difficulties are more related to not paying attention to details or being overly active, which directly corresponds to the symptom of making careless mistakes or failing to give close attention to details.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but the details really do trip me up quite a bit. Like, when I help out with the volunteer storytelling flyers down at the center, or when I'm writing down my garden notes, I’ll just completely miss a date, or I'll leave out somebody's name. Or I'll measure something wrong out in the yard, even though I could have sworn I looked it over real careful. 

Speaking of the yard, I was measuring for some new tomato stakes recently. I grow those big heirloom tomatoes, the Brandywines. They get so heavy you have to tie them up to the stakes with strips of old pantyhose so the stems don't snap. My grandmother taught me that trick. She had a garden the size of a baseball diamond out behind her place. Grew absolutely everything under the sun. Corn, squash, pole beans. She used to can her own green beans in those heavy glass mason jars. You'd sit in the kitchen and just wait to hear that sharp little "pop" sound when the lids sealed as they cooled down on the counter. 

We kept all those jars down in the root cellar. That cellar always smelled like damp earth and old potatoes. There was an old iron coal chute down there, too, from back before they put the oil furnace in. The coal truck would pull right up to the side of the house and just rattle all that coal right down the chute. It made a terrible racket, and the coal dust would get on absolutely everything. You'd be wiping black soot off the windowsills for a week after a delivery. 

Wait, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Losing the track. What was it you were asking me about? Oh, right, the details or being restless. Yeah, it's the details that get me. Just missing dates on those flyers and messing up my garden measurements, mostly, no matter how hard I try to double-check things.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties with focusing and sitting still might be related to ADHD?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the patient's opinion on whether their symptoms are related to ADHD, which is a general question about insight and diagnosis rather than a specific symptom from the profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't really know. I mean, I've heard the term before, mostly on the television or when people talk about kids in school. But for me? I'm not sure. It's just... the way I am, I guess. 

Speaking of television, they just don't make shows like they used to, do they? Everything now is all these reality programs with people yelling at each other on islands or in big houses. Or it's those crime shows where they solve a murder in forty-five minutes using some fancy computer that can zoom in on a reflection in a puddle from a satellite. Back in the day, you had proper stories. Like *Gunsmoke* or *The Andy Griffith Show*. 

Andy Griffith, now there was a show. Just a sheriff and his boy, and Barney Fife causing all sorts of trouble. Don Knotts was a genius, absolute genius. The way he could just shake and look nervous, it was pure comedy. My dad used to laugh so hard at Barney Fife that he'd start coughing and have to go get a glass of water. 

My dad drank a lot of water. Always had a big glass jar of it in the fridge with a slice of lemon in it. He said the lemon cut the dust from the factory. He worked at the old textile mill over in the next county. Spun cotton mostly, I think. The noise in that place was deafening. He had to wear these big heavy earmuffs all day, but he still lost most of his hearing by the time he was fifty. He used to say he didn't mind, though, because it meant he didn't have to listen to my mother's soap operas. 

She loved her stories, my mother. *Days of Our Lives*, *General Hospital*. She'd iron clothes in the living room just so she wouldn't miss a minute of it. The smell of hot iron on damp cotton... that always takes me right back to being a kid. 

But, uh... I lost the thread again, didn't I? You were asking about that ADHD thing. Yeah, I really don't know if that's what it is. I haven't really thought about it having a name like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily related to inattention or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your main difficulty is with staying focused on tasks or with feeling restless and fidgety?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: Sitting through a quiet meeting or church talk, I feel like I’ve got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch even when I know I should stay put.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks whether the main difficulty is focusing on tasks or feeling restless and fidgety, which directly maps to the symptom of feeling restless.

patient.answer:
Well, I'd say the restlessness is a pretty big one for me. Like, if I'm sitting through a quiet meeting or a church talk, I just feel like I’ve got to shift around in my seat, or I'll start tapping my foot. I just get this overwhelming urge to get up and stretch, even when I know I really should just stay put and be polite. 

Speaking of church, our pastor, Reverend Davis, he can really stretch a sermon out. Nice man, though. His wife plays the organ. It's one of those beautiful old pipe organs, you know the kind? With all the wooden pedals and the big brass pipes up on the wall. They had to get a specialist all the way from Chicago just to come tune the thing last spring. Cost the congregation a small fortune. We had to do a whole month of bake sales just to cover the travel expenses for the tuning fella. 

I made three cherry pies for that sale. Used my mother's old recipe. The secret is a little bit of almond extract in the filling, it really makes the cherries pop. And you have to use real lard in the crust. People are so scared of lard these days, but it's what makes the pastry actually flake. You cut it in ice-cold with a pastry blender, and you have to use ice water, too, or the fat melts before it even hits the oven... 

Wait, goodness, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry, I get to talking about baking and I just lose the whole point of the conversation. You were asking about the fidgeting. But yes, it's definitely the restlessness. Sitting in those pews or anywhere quiet, I just can't keep my feet still to save my life.
